red.focus: Understand why a legal system may divide decisions between local and national institutions.
red.summary: Local authorities may know community needs, while a central government can coordinate problems crossing many boundaries. Learn why the right decision maker depends on legal authority and the problem's scale.
checklist: I can identify an advantage of local decision-making
I can explain why some problems need wider coordination
I can check which institution is lawfully responsible

sections.title: The local perspective can help
sections.body_md: A town knows where children walk to school and which crossings are dangerous. Local officials may respond faster than a distant ministry because residents can describe hazards directly. But local power comes from law, and decisions may be constrained by national rights protections. A town cannot necessarily make any rule it wants just because a majority favors it. The question is which level has the responsibility, evidence, and authority to act while protecting every person affected.
sections.audio_script: A town knows where children walk to school and which crossings are dangerous. The question is which level has the responsibility, evidence, and authority to act while protecting every person affected.

sections.title: Some problems cross borders
sections.body_md: Smoke from one town's factory can drift into several neighboring towns. A rule made only by the town hosting the factory may ignore people downwind. Regional or national coordination can prevent gaps and conflicting requirements. Central decisions can also be insensitive to local conditions. A wise system identifies what cannot be achieved reliably at one level and what can. Uniform rules are sometimes important for basic rights, even when the practical details of implementation remain local.

sections.title: Power must remain answerable
sections.body_md: A resident needs to know which office can correct a dangerous intersection or remedy illegal discrimination. Fragmented authority can produce confusion if each institution blames another. Clear assignments, accessible complaints, and cooperation make the division of power more useful. A strong beginner's answer asks who makes the rule, who applies it, who pays for it, and who reviews a violation. The legal framework differs among countries; no single model of local government fits all legal orders.

yellow.focus: Distinguish federalism, unitary administration, and legal subsidiarity.
yellow.summary: Federalism distributes constitutionally protected powers, while a unitary system may delegate authority by ordinary law. Subsidiarity provides a reason to prefer decisions near affected people when wider action is not necessary.
checklist: I can distinguish federal and delegated arrangements
I can explain subsidiarity without promising unconditional local autonomy
I can analyze a rights conflict across different legal levels

sections.title: Federalism is a constitutional choice
sections.body_md: In many federations, a constitution divides governing powers between a national government and constituent states or provinces. A unitary state may assign local powers through legislation that can be altered according to its legal system. The distinction affects how conflicts are resolved and which institutions can claim final authority in particular matters. Federalism does not mean that every matter is local, nor that national government lacks necessary coordinating responsibilities. A lawyer must read the relevant constitution rather than assume an idealized diagram.
sections.audio_script: In many federations, a constitution divides governing powers between a national government and constituent states or provinces. A unitary state may assign local powers through legislation that can be altered according to its legal system. The distinction affects how conflicts are resolved and which institutions can claim final authority in particular matters. Federalism does not mean that every matter is local, nor that national government lacks necessary coordinating responsibilities. A lawyer must read the relevant constitution rather than assume an idealized diagram.

sections.title: Subsidiarity asks where action works
sections.body_md: Subsidiarity generally favors handling a task at the lowest effective level, while recognizing that broader institutions may be necessary. It is a normative design principle in some contexts and a treaty-based legal standard in others. An individual city's vaccination effort could be appropriate locally; coordinating cross-border disease reporting may need a wider framework. The analysis should ask whether local actors can achieve the objective and whether higher-level involvement adds genuine value. Closeness to citizens is not the same as adequacy of action.

sections.title: Protect rights across institutional borders
sections.body_md: One province may seek a different school curriculum while the constitution protects a common baseline of nondiscrimination. Regional variation can reflect genuine needs, but higher law may constrain what local authorities can do. Conflicts require a hierarchy or competence rule, not a declaration that either diversity or uniformity is always better. A sound case analysis identifies the power assigned to each level, the protected individual interests, and the institution authorized to decide the dispute.

orange.focus: Apply EU conferral, subsidiarity and proportionality without confusing them.
orange.summary: Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union separates whether the Union has a power from whether and how it may exercise it. Evaluate action in nonexclusive competences using an evidence-based comparison of national and Union capacity.
checklist: I can state conferral as a threshold to EU action
I can apply Article 5(3) subsidiarity only within its proper domain
I can distinguish subsidiarity from proportionality

sections.title: Conferral comes before preferred outcomes
sections.body_md: Under Article 5(2) TEU, the Union acts within competences conferred upon it by the Member States in the Treaties. A desirable policy does not create competence. The first step in any EU proposal is therefore to identify the treaty basis and scope. A government might want Union-wide building codes, but it must show lawful authority rather than rely on the benefits of consistency alone. Competence cannot be inferred just from economic or technological importance.
sections.audio_script: Under Article 5(2) TEU, the Union acts within competences conferred upon it by the Member States in the Treaties. A desirable policy does not create competence. The first step in any EU proposal is therefore to identify the treaty basis and scope. A government might want Union-wide building codes, but it must show lawful authority rather than rely on the benefits of consistency alone. Competence cannot be inferred just from economic or technological importance.

sections.title: Subsidiarity tests nonexclusive action
sections.body_md: Article 5(3) TEU applies where Union competence is not exclusive. It asks whether objectives cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States, including their central, regional and local levels, and can be better achieved at Union level because of scale or effects. Evidence about cross-border spillovers and the capacity of national measures is therefore relevant. This test is not a general power to intervene whenever Brussels prefers uniformity. Nor does it convert nonexclusive areas into subjects that must always stay local.
sections.audio_script: Article 5(3) TEU applies where Union competence is not exclusive. It asks whether objectives cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States, including their central, regional and local levels, and can be better achieved at Union level because of scale or effects. Evidence about cross-border spillovers and the capacity of national measures is therefore relevant. This test is not a general power to intervene whenever Brussels prefers uniformity. Nor does it convert nonexclusive areas into subjects that must always stay local.

sections.title: Proportionality tests the chosen means
sections.body_md: Article 5(4) TEU requires that the content and form of Union action not exceed what is necessary to achieve treaty objectives. An EU measure may have an appropriate legal basis and satisfy subsidiarity yet still be overbroad in the means it selects. The decision maker must separately examine scope, objectives, affected rights, and less intrusive options where the governing method requires. Distinguish the three tests in writing: may the Union act, should this objective be pursued at Union level, and how far may the measure go?

black.focus: Defend multilevel authority that preserves local voice, common rights, and Indigenous self-government.
black.summary: Decentralization can increase participation or conceal local domination, while centralization can secure equal protection or erase distinct legal orders. Design an allocation of authority that treats communities as participants rather than administrative units.
checklist: I can critique purely geographical allocation of governing power
I can evaluate Indigenous jurisdiction and legal pluralism with institutional care
I can propose accountable cooperation and rights protection across levels

sections.title: Location alone does not guarantee democracy
sections.body_md: A small municipality may be close to residents but controlled by a local elite that excludes newcomers or minorities. A distant national institution may be less responsive but better able to protect minimum rights. Conversely, centralized rule may ignore cultural traditions and legitimate demands for local self-determination. A doctoral analysis distinguishes the physical scale of government from actual participation, rights protection, and administrative competence. It asks who can influence decisions, who bears harms, and whose appeals are heard.

sections.title: Plural law can distribute authority differently
sections.body_md: Indigenous communities may possess legal traditions and institutions that predate the state, but constitutional and treaty recognition varies. Treating all such institutions as optional local agencies can misdescribe self-government; assuming every Indigenous legal rule has the same legal force everywhere is equally mistaken. Explore legally recognized jurisdiction, consultation, conflicting rights, and enforcement arrangements in the specific place. The goal is not romanticizing pluralism but taking seriously who has the authority and lived legitimacy to make and apply law.

sections.title: Design an accountable shared structure
sections.body_md: Imagine flood protection spanning several regions, including an Indigenous territory. A legitimate plan identifies statutory or treaty competences, local participation, wider coordination needs, clear funding responsibilities, and independent review. It should allow knowledge from affected communities to shape implementation without letting any institution evade responsibility for harm. Specify which powers existing law supplies and which require negotiated or legislative reform. Measure outcomes for smaller communities as well as the central budget. Good multilevel government is power allocated with reasons and checked against the people it governs.
